title: An armillary sphere
alt: An armillary sphere on a wooden stand: a fixed horizon ring and an upright meridian ring hold a polar axis tilted at 21°, about which a cage of rings turns: the celestial equator, the tropics, the polar circles, two colures and the broad tilted band of the ecliptic, with a small Earth at the centre.

scale.note: A desk instrument about 74 cm tall. The Earth at the centre is drawn far larger than it would be at the scale of the sky.

parts.name: Base
parts.note: A turned foot that keeps the instrument level, so the horizon ring lies flat.

parts.name: Pillar
parts.note: The turned column that carries the meridian ring in its cradle and the four arms of the horizon ring.

parts.name: Cradle
parts.note: Two cheeks that hold the meridian ring upright in the plane running north and south.

parts.name: Horizon arms
parts.note: Four curved arms from the pillar that hold the horizon ring level.

parts.name: Horizon ring
parts.note: The observer’s horizon: the sky above its plane can be seen, the half below cannot. Its marks give the directions of the compass.

parts.name: Meridian ring
parts.note: The great circle through the poles and the point overhead, running north and south. It holds the polar axis, and its degrees set the latitude.

parts.name: Meridian clamps
parts.note: Where the meridian ring passes the horizon ring, north and south: they hold the two at right angles.

parts.name: Polar axis
parts.note: The axis the sky turns about, pointing at the celestial poles. It rises above the north horizon by the observer’s latitude: 21° for Hà Nội.

parts.name: Earth
parts.note: A small Earth at the centre, as in Ptolemy’s picture of the cosmos: the sky turns around it, it stays still.

parts.name: Pole bearings
parts.note: Sleeves on the polar axis where the colures meet, at the celestial poles: the whole cage turns on them.

parts.name: Solstitial colure
parts.note: The great circle through the celestial poles and the two solstices, where the ecliptic is farthest from the equator.

parts.name: Equinoctial colure
parts.note: The great circle through the celestial poles and the two equinoxes, where the ecliptic crosses the equator.

parts.name: Celestial equator
parts.note: Earth’s equator projected on the sky, halfway between the poles. Its 24 marks are the hours of the sky’s daily turn.

parts.name: Tropic of Cancer
parts.note: The circle 23.44° north of the equator: the Sun reaches it at the June solstice, its farthest north.

parts.name: Tropic of Capricorn
parts.note: The circle 23.44° south of the equator: the Sun reaches it at the December solstice, its farthest south.

parts.name: Arctic circle
parts.note: The circle 23.44° from the north celestial pole (66.56° north).

parts.name: Antarctic circle
parts.note: The circle 23.44° from the south celestial pole (66.56° south).

parts.name: Ecliptic
parts.note: The Sun’s yearly path among the stars, tilted 23.44° to the equator. The band is the zodiac, cut into twelve signs of 30°.

dimensions.name: the latitude: the height of the celestial pole above the horizon
the tilt of the ecliptic to the equator

steps.title: An armillary sphere
steps.text: A model of the sky made of rings, each one a circle that astronomers draw on the sky. A small Earth sits at the centre, as in Ptolemy’s picture of the cosmos.

steps.title: Horizon and meridian
steps.text: These rings stay still. The horizon ring splits the sky we see from the half below; the upright meridian ring runs north and south through the point overhead. The axis rises above the north horizon by the latitude: 21° for Hà Nội.

steps.title: The sky turns
steps.text: Everything inside the meridian turns about the polar axis, once a day, east to west. The celestial equator turns in its own plane, halfway between the poles; its 24 marks are hours.

steps.title: Tropics and polar circles
steps.text: Four smaller circles run parallel to the equator: the tropics, 23.44° north and south of it, which the Sun reaches at the solstices; and the polar circles, 23.44° from the poles.

steps.title: The ecliptic
steps.text: The broad band is the ecliptic, the Sun’s path through the year, tilted 23.44° to the equator. It touches the tropics at the solstices and crosses the equator at the equinoxes, where the two colures cross it.
